# MedBayes-Lite as Clinical Uncertainty Governance: Experimental Summary

*Generated by the `medbayes_eval/` pipeline. Every number below is from real models on
real medical data (no hand-set values). Run date: 2026-06-14.*

This study repositions MedBayes-Lite away from "another uncertainty-aware attention
method" and toward a **clinical uncertainty governance** framework, and asks whether
the evidence actually supports that framing. It does, but with important and honest
qualifications that should reshape the paper's claims.

---

## TL;DR (the five headline questions)

| # | Question | Verdict | Strength |
|---|----------|---------|----------|
| 1 | Does MedBayes-Lite reduce **harmful overconfident** clinical errors? | **Yes**, strongly, where the base model is overconfident | High (p≈0) |
| 2 | Does it **abstain more appropriately** on ambiguous/high-risk cases? | **Yes**, but via confidence deflation + thresholding, not better error ranking | Medium |
| 3 | Does it improve **risk-coverage** trade-offs (AURC)? | **No** meaningful change; temperature scaling matches it; ensembles beat it on ranking | High (null) |
| 4 | Does it stay useful under **medical domain shift**? | **Yes**, this is its strongest result | High |
| 5 | Are **CUS and ZTI** meaningful summaries? | **CUS yes (keep), ZTI weak (demote)** | High |

**One-sentence reframing for the paper:** MedBayes-Lite is best presented as a
*calibration-and-abstention governance layer* that prevents confident clinical errors
(especially under distribution shift), not as a method that improves the model's
underlying ability to rank its own errors.

---

## Setup

- **Datasets:** MedMCQA (4-way, n=3,683 test), MedQA-USMLE (4-way, n=973 test; also the
  OOD target), PubMedQA (3-way, n=350 test). MediQ + MIMIC adapters are wired but not in
  this slice (MIMIC needs credentialed access; MediQ is a reformatting of MedQA).
- **Models:** strong pretrained MedMCQA multiple-choice checkpoints (BioBERT,
  PubMedBERT) for the MCQ tasks; a locally fine-tuned encoder family (BERT-base, BioBERT,
  Bio_ClinicalBERT, PubMedBERT, one identical routine) for PubMedQA; and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
  (local generative) with API-compatible UQ. 3 seeds; MC-dropout = 15 samples.
- **UQ methods:** base/MSP, temperature scaling, MC-dropout, conformal (split LAC), deep
  ensemble (PubMedQA, fine-tuned seeds), **MedBayes-Lite** (MC-dropout BMA + calibration +
  confidence-guided abstention); generative self-consistency, semantic entropy, verbalized.
- **Buckets:** 13 rule-based clinical categories with severity weights; "harmful
  overconfident error" = wrong AND confidence>=tau AND severity>=2.5.
- **Confidence convention:** calibrated max predictive probability for all encoder methods
  (so ECE/coverage are comparable); a method's distinctive signal lives in its uncertainty
  and abstention behavior.

---

## Q1. Harmful overconfident error reduction — **YES (strong)**

On tasks where the base model is overconfident, MedBayes-Lite removes nearly all harmful
overconfident errors, and temperature scaling captures most of the same gain.

| Dataset | Model | Method | ECE | harmful@0.8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MedMCQA | PubMedBERT | base | 0.255 | 0.056 |
| MedMCQA | PubMedBERT | temp_scaling | 0.081 | 0.012 |
| MedMCQA | PubMedBERT | **MedBayes-Lite** | **0.023** | **0.003** |
| MedMCQA | BioBERT | base | 0.317 | 0.067 |
| MedMCQA | BioBERT | **MedBayes-Lite** | **0.021** | **0.000** |

Paired bootstrap (base minus MedBayes-Lite, positive = improvement), n=2,000:
- harmful@0.8 reduction **+0.053 to +0.217**, p≈0 across all four MCQ settings.
- ECE reduction **+0.23 to +0.33**, p≈0.

**Caveat (important):** this reduction is driven by **calibration + confidence
deflation**, not by the model getting better at knowing when it is wrong (see Q3). It is
real and clinically valuable, but the mechanism should be described honestly.

---

## Q2. Appropriate abstention on ambiguous/high-risk cases — **YES (mechanistically nuanced)**

- Selective accuracy on accepted predictions rises sharply: on MedMCQA/PubMedBERT,
  accepted accuracy at tau=0.7 goes from 0.571 (base) to **0.818** (MedBayes-Lite); on
  BioBERT, 0.457 to **0.714**. The model answers less often but is right more often when it does.
- Abstention **recall** (fraction of wrong predictions that get deferred) at tau=0.7 reaches
  **0.97-0.99** for MedBayes-Lite vs ~0.55 for base.
- **Honest cost:** coverage at tau=0.7 collapses (e.g. 0.54 to 0.10 on MedMCQA). MedBayes-Lite
  buys safety with a large reduction in how often it is willing to answer. On a hard 4-way
  exam this is defensible ("when in doubt, defer"), but the coverage cost must be reported,
  not hidden.

**Bucket-level harmful errors** (`results/metrics/metrics_by_bucket.csv`,
`results/plots/bucketwise_harmful_bar.png`): base harmful overconfidence concentrates in the
high-severity / diagnosis / treatment / medication buckets; MedBayes-Lite drives these toward
zero. This is the clearest "governance" visual for the paper.

---

## Q3. Risk-coverage / AURC — **NO improvement (the critical, honest finding)**

This is the result that should most change the paper.

| Dataset | Model | base AURC | MedBayes-Lite AURC | base AUROC-error | MBL AUROC-error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MedMCQA | PubMedBERT | 0.376 | 0.392 | 0.675 | 0.662 |
| MedMCQA | BioBERT | 0.517 | 0.521 | 0.603 | 0.607 |
| MedQA | PubMedBERT | 0.539 | 0.554 | 0.567 | 0.570 |

Paired bootstrap on AURC: **non-significant** in 3 of 4 MCQ settings (p = 0.64–0.96), and
*slightly worse* in one (PubMedBERT/MedMCQA, +0.016, p≈0). Error-ranking AUROC is flat or
marginally lower under MedBayes-Lite.

**Interpretation:** MC-dropout averaging + calibration changes the *confidence scale* (fixing
ECE and harmful-overconfidence-at-threshold) but does **not** improve the *ordering* of
predictions by reliability. A perfectly calibrated and a poorly calibrated model can share the
same AURC. So:
- Do **not** claim MedBayes-Lite improves selective prediction / error detection in general.
- Temperature scaling alone achieves comparable calibration at a fraction of the cost; on
  PubMedQA, **deep ensembles** achieve the best AURC (0.345–0.363 vs 0.371–0.394 base),
  which MedBayes-Lite does not match. Ranking gains come from ensembling, calibration gains
  from temperature/MC, and MedBayes-Lite is essentially MC-dropout + calibration.

---

## Q4. Robustness under medical domain shift — **YES (strongest result)**

Transfer: models trained on MedMCQA, evaluated out-of-distribution on MedQA-USMLE
(`results/metrics/ood_transfer.csv`).

| Model | Method | ID ECE | OOD ECE | ECE drift | OOD harmful@0.8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PubMedBERT | base | 0.255 | 0.325 | +0.070 | **0.213** |
| PubMedBERT | **MedBayes-Lite** | 0.030 | 0.055 | **+0.026** | **0.002** |
| BioBERT | base | 0.317 | 0.410 | +0.093 | **0.217** |
| BioBERT | **MedBayes-Lite** | 0.015 | 0.084 | +0.069 | **0.000** |

Under domain shift the base models become **dangerously overconfident: ~21% of high-severity
items are confident errors**. MedBayes-Lite contains this almost entirely (harmful → ~0) and
roughly halves the calibration drift. This is the most compelling clinical-governance argument
in the study and should be a headline figure (risk-coverage + harmful-bucket bars, ID vs OOD).

---

## Q5. Are CUS and ZTI meaningful? — **CUS yes (keep), ZTI weak (demote)**

Correlation across 739 model×method×bucket groups (`results/metrics/cus_zti_correlation.csv`):

**CUS is a valid clinical-calibration summary:**
- vs harmful@0.8: Pearson **r = 0.88** (p≈1e-241)
- vs severity-weighted error: **r = 0.90**
- vs abstention recall: **r = −0.81**
- vs AURC: r = 0.24 (weak — CUS is a calibration metric, not a ranking metric, as expected)

**ZTI is weak and threshold-confounded:**
- vs AURC: r = −0.70 (its only strong correlate, and AURC is already a standard metric)
- vs selective accuracy: r = 0.34; vs coverage: Pearson 0.26 but **Spearman −0.05** (no
  monotone relationship — ZTI's coverage/accuracy harmonic mean is unstable across operating points)

**Recommendation:** Keep **CUS** as a secondary, severity-aware calibration score (it cleanly
tracks harmful overconfidence). **Demote ZTI**: report standard AURC + selective accuracy +
coverage-at-threshold instead; ZTI adds no information beyond AURC and is sensitive to tau.

---

## Generative model (Qwen2.5-7B): a cautionary contrast

| Dataset | Method | acc | ECE | harmful@0.8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PubMedQA | self_consistency | 0.525 | 0.445 | **0.360** |
| PubMedQA | verbalized | 0.650 | 0.167 | 0.110 |
| MedQA | self_consistency | 0.685 | 0.307 | 0.265 |
| MedMCQA | self_consistency | 0.495 | 0.484 | 0.115 |

The instruction-tuned generative model is **far more dangerous than the encoders**: on
PubMedQA it is confidently wrong on **36%** of high-severity items, and self-consistency does
**not** fix this (it is overconfident *and* self-consistent). Interestingly, **verbalized
confidence** ("state your confidence") calibrates substantially better than self-consistency
(ECE 0.167 vs 0.445). Note Qwen's uncertainty *ranks* errors well on PubMedQA (AUROC-error
0.78), so the failure is purely a miscalibrated confidence scale, exactly the regime where a
governance/abstention layer is needed. This strengthens the paper's motivation: API-class
clinical models need explicit uncertainty governance, and naive self-consistency is insufficient.

---

## Perturbation sensitivity (MedBayes-Lite, MedMCQA, n=300)

`results/metrics/perturbation_report.csv`. Confidence drop / abstention increase under
controlled clinical corruptions:

| Perturbation | confidence drop | abstention increase | flip rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| add irrelevant distractor | 0.051 | 0.073 | 0.37 |
| add contradictory symptom | 0.033 | 0.060 | 0.34 |
| remove key evidence | 0.015 | 0.037 | 0.19 |
| remove lab value | 0.006 | 0.017 | 0.16 |
| **alter numeric value** | **−0.001** | 0.013 | 0.14 |
| **vague evidence** | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.16 |

MedBayes-Lite appropriately raises uncertainty for distractors and contradictions, but is
**insensitive to numeric/vital-value corruption** (confidence does not drop when a lab value
is made clinically implausible) and to vagueness. This is an honest, clinically important
limitation: the framework governs *aggregate* predictive uncertainty but does not detect
local numeric implausibility, which matters for dosing and lab interpretation.

---

## What this means for the rewrite (concrete)

**Claims to make (supported):**
1. MedBayes-Lite is a clinical *uncertainty governance* layer that drives harmful
   overconfident errors toward zero (p≈0), most importantly **under domain shift** (21% → ~0).
2. It substantially improves calibration (ECE −0.23 to −0.33) and the reliability of accepted
   predictions (selective accuracy +0.15 to +0.25).
3. CUS is a validated severity-aware calibration summary (r≈0.88 with harmful overconfidence).
4. Naive generative self-consistency does **not** confer safety; governance/abstention is needed.

**Claims to drop or soften (not supported):**
1. Do not claim improved selective prediction / error ranking / AURC. It is flat (and
   temperature scaling or ensembles match or beat it).
2. Do not present the "overconfidence reduction" as discrimination; it is calibration plus
   coverage reduction. Report the coverage cost.
3. Do not headline ZTI; demote it to an appendix or replace with AURC + selective accuracy.
4. The original "32–48% overconfidence reduction" framing should be restated as
   *calibration-error and harmful-error reduction at fixed operating points*, with the
   AURC-null result stated explicitly.

**Honest negative/limitations to include:**
- Null result on PubMedQA (models already well-calibrated/underconfident → MedBayes-Lite adds
  nothing; harmful errors already 0).
- Insensitivity to numeric-value corruption and vagueness.
- MedBayes-Lite ≈ MC-dropout + temperature; ablate this explicitly so reviewers see the
  marginal contribution of each component.

---

## Reproduce / scale

```bash
python -m medbayes_eval.run all --config configs/default.yaml   # encoders + ood + perturb + analyze
python -m medbayes_eval.run_generative --datasets pubmedqa medmcqa medqa --n 200 --samples 10
```
Outputs in `results/` (raw_predictions, metrics, plots, tables, statistical_tests,
bucket_assignments). Scale up by setting `seeds: [0,1,2,3,4]` and `max_eval: null`. Add the
MIMIC mortality axis via the credentialed adapter in `data/loaders.py::load_mimic`.

## Caveats on this slice
- 3 seeds (not 5); deterministic methods have zero seed variance on the pretrained MCQ
  checkpoints (their variance comes from sampling; CIs come from the per-sample bootstrap).
- Generative slice is 200 items/dataset (cost). Encoders use full test splits.
- The external PubMedQA checkpoint `blizrys/...-pubmedqa` was **dropped**: it had a reversed
  label space (11.4% accuracy, recoverable to 60.9% only with a manual class permutation), a
  cautionary example of reusing HF checkpoints without verifying label order. PubMedQA results
  use our own identically-trained encoder family instead.
